summary: Technical deep dive focused on embeddings and reranking performance & cost tradeoffs. transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna go deep on embeddings and reranking perf and cost. Marcus will drive the SE bits.
[00:00:15] Marcus Hill: Hey all, hi Priya, Tom, Anita. Quick agenda: talk dims, batching, kv cache, quant, and then costs + recommended configs for SLOs.
[00:00:30] Priya Sharma: Hi, thanks. Our goal is sub-50ms tail for single-shot rerank at 8 candidates but scale to bursts of 500 qps for bulk.
[00:00:45] Tom Becker: Also we're on VPC-only, need to understand network egress and on-prem options.
[00:01:05] Marcus: Got it. Quick question on current baseline: Rajiv, what embedding dims and infra do you use today?
[00:01:25] Rajiv Menon: We're using 768-dim from open model x2, hosted on self-managed infra - 4x A10s, batching size about 64 for generation, but for embedding create we do batch 128. Reranking is a follow-up step in our pipeline.
[00:01:40] Speaker 1: (inaudible) some requests are latency-sensitive, others are offline.
[00:01:55] Marcus: Cool. So main tradeoffs: vector dims -> quality vs compute & memory; batch sizes -> throughput vs tail latency; kv cache mostly applies to decoder models but for reranking when we do cross-encoder or full model scoring similar cache and memory patterns.
[00:02:20] Priya: For rerank we're primarily doing dot-product scoring of candidate embeddings, occasionally cross-encoder for high-precision.
[00:02:35] Lena: For dot product recall tasks, 1536-dim gave consistent lift in our tests for your domain, but cost goes up roughly linearly in vector ops and storage.
[00:02:50] Tom: Can we quantify? Per-embedding cost and per-rerank cost?
[00:03:05] Marcus: Ballpark: compute FLOPs scale with dim. Storage and memory for ANN indices scale with dim too. If you double dims from 768 to 1536, inference compute roughly doubles and memory for indices doubles; throughput per GPU drops ~50% if everything else held constant. But you gain accuracy often diminishing returns past 1536.
[00:03:30] Priya: What about latency SLOs? We're aiming 95th < 50ms for online ranked response.
[00:03:45] Marcus: For pure dot-product scoring (vector lookup + dot on CPU or small GPU op) you can get sub-10ms per candidate if index is in-memory on the same node. But network hops and serialization add overhead. On hosted Redwood with dedicated capacity, a 1536-dim dot for 8 candidates median is ~12-18ms, 95th ~25-40ms depending on batching and placement.
[00:04:10] Anita Rao: Wait that seems optimistic, what's the assumption for batch size?
[00:04:20] Marcus: Those numbers are single-request, no batching for scoring, index in RAM and colocated on the same rack. If you add batching to score many queries together you can amortize overhead: batch 32 could reduce per-query tokenized overhead but increases tail.
[00:04:40] Rajiv: We worry about cold starts and KV cache warmup for cross-encoder runs.
[00:04:55] Marcus: Cross-encoders are heavier. KV cache matters if you're reusing contexts; for rerank scoring with short contexts cache benefit limited. But for long query+doc pairs it helps. On quantized models, KV cache footprint shrinks but decoding arithmetic changes latency slightly.
[00:05:20] Priya: Can you explain quantization tradeoffs for embeddings? We were considering 8-bit or 4-bit to cut memory.
[00:05:35] Marcus: Sure. For embedding extraction, we often quantize encoder-only weights to 8-bit without large quality hit. For 4-bit, you need more careful calibration; sometimes works for retrieval but can degrade similarity for fine-grained rerank. In our tests 8-bit for 1536-dim preserved >99% of cosine similarity vs fp16, 4-bit dropped ~1-3% depending on model and calibration.
[00:06:00] Tom: Does quantization change inference latency?
[00:06:10] Marcus: On many runtimes, 8-bit kernels are faster and reduce memory bandwidth; net latency improves 10-25% for throughput-bound workloads. But on some hardware 4-bit kernels require specialized ops and sometimes slower if kernels not optimized.
[00:06:30] Speaker 1: (overlap) so there is vendor variance.
[00:06:40] Lena: Also consider index type: HNSW vs IVF+PQ. PQ pairs well with quantized vectors to reduce disk/memory. HNSW uses more memory but has lower latency for high-recall.
[00:06:55] Priya: We currently run HNSW, memory is ballooning. Would PQ+IVF with 1536 dims be sensible?
[00:07:10] Marcus: Yes, IVF+PQ reduces memory by compressing vectors; you pay slightly higher latencies and potential recall drop. For large corpora (50k-1M docs) PQ shines. For your 50k prototype, HNSW may be fine; for production 500k+, move to IVF+PQ and measure recall-vs-latency.
[00:07:35] Anita: Latency SLO under VPC — how much network overhead do we expect between Redis/ANN store and inference?
[00:07:50] Marcus: If colocated in VPC private subnet, single-digit ms. Across regions or across cloud provider boundary add 10-30ms depending on topology. That's why we recommend co-locating index and inference for latency-critical paths.
[00:08:10] Priya: On dedicated vs hosted: cost differences?
[00:08:20] Lena: Hosted is usage-based: you pay per-embedding + per-rerank compute. Dedicated is committed capacity, better for predictable bursts and avoids per-token variability. We provided a kilotoken cost sheet — we'll update it for embedding dims. For 1536 dims, hosted per-embedding compute cost ~1.9x compared to 768 in our pricing model.
[00:08:45] Rajiv: For benchmarking, Marcus, what config do you recommend we run?
[00:08:55] Marcus: Run three dims: 512, 768, 1536. For each, run a 10k-query rerank: 8 candidates online, and a bulk throughput test at 500 qps for 10 minutes. Measure tail latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput per GPU, and memory footprint for index. We'll provision a dedicated instance to mirror your VPC topology.
[00:09:20] Tom: If we do VPC-hosted Redwood private, how is KMS handled?
[00:09:30] Lena: We integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping, and on-prem uses HSM if required. Security docs will be shared.
[00:09:45] Priya: For the rerank step, sometimes we do re-ranking with a cross-encoder only for top-20 candidates. How does that change recommended batch sizes?
[00:10:00] Marcus: Cross-encoders are heavier: batch for latency-bound requests is tricky — we recommend micro-batching of 4-8 to keep tail low. For bulk offline, batch 32-64. Use async workers to hide latency. Also consider early-exit heuristics: do embedding first for top-K and only if confidence low run cross-encoder.
[00:10:25] Speaker 1: What about KV cache reuse patterns for cross-encoder?
[00:10:35] Marcus: If queries share prefixes (e.g., same query with different docs), KV cache helps. Otherwise each pair is unique and cache hit low. For rerank, kv caching usually less effective unless you replicate contexts.
[00:10:55] Priya: Can Redwood run the benchmark within our VPC?
[00:11:05] Marcus: Yes, through our private deployment we can deploy a temporary dedicated node in your VPC or allow you to run the Redwood benchmarking container on-prem with our SE assistance. For speed, we can run an initial hosted benchmark and then a VPC run.
[00:11:25] Lena: We'll need a sample dataset — around 50k docs ideally — and a set of 10k queries. Priya: we'll try to share that.
[00:11:40] Anita: Any gotchas with batching and tail latency at 500 qps bursts?
[00:11:55] Marcus: Bursty traffic is the tricky part: autoscaling reaction time, queueing at the runtime, and batching algorithms. Continuous batching reduces GPU idle but increases worst-case tail. For strict SLOs, configure max batch latency and a lower max batch size, or use priority lanes: small batch lane for interactive and large batch lane for offline. Redwood runtime supports lane-based routing.
[00:12:20] Rajiv: How do we size dedicated capacity? We want to avoid overcommit but not see queueing spikes.
[00:12:30] Marcus: We model your 95th qps and estimate GPU throughput for the model/quantization/batch size. We'll send a sizing calc: roughly, 1 A100 equivalent can handle X embeddings/sec at dim 1536 with 8-bit quant and batching 256 (for offline), but interactive small-batch throughput much lower. We'll propose a base pool plus burst nodes.
[00:12:55] Priya: Any recommendations on embedding dimensionality for healthcare-ish semantic search?
[00:13:05] Marcus: For clinical notes and shorter docs, 768 often hits a good sweet spot; for multi-entity semantic needs and high recall, 1536 shows uplift. You should run A/B eval on your tasks.
[00:13:20] Tom: On costs — what's the biggest levers?
[00:13:30] Marcus: Key levers: dims, quantization, batching strategy, and routing (only run cross-encoder when needed). Also caching and prefix reuse reduce cost. Index compression saves storage & memory cost.
[00:13:45] Lena: We'll attach the cost calc and a short checklist for moving to VPC/private.
[00:13:55] Priya: Let's talk about latency numbers again — if we aim 95th <50ms for 8 candidates using 1536 dims, is that realistic in a private deployment?
[00:14:10] Marcus: Yes, if index and inference are colocated, using low-latency storage (in-memory) and small-batch scoring. Expect p95 around 30-45ms in that scenario. If index is remote or on disk, add 10-30ms.
[00:14:30] Anita: Will quantization introduce nondeterminism in similarity scores across runs?
[00:14:40] Marcus: Minor variability yes, usually stable. But calibration step required. For regulated workflows, keep an unquantized reference for audit.
[00:14:55] Speaker 1: How about embedding serving patterns — do you recommend vector DBs or custom in-memory stores?
[00:15:05] Marcus: Vector DBs (Pinecone, FAISS, Milvus) or managed Redwood index depending on scale. For 50k-1M docs, many teams prefer tuned FAISS with IVF+PQ for cost. Redwood can manage the index in dedicated private deployments too.
[00:15:25] Priya: Any tips on measuring recall vs latency tradeoff in A/B?
[00:15:35] Marcus: Capture offline eval metrics (mrr, recall@k) and latency buckets; run ablations across dims/quant/index type; use calibration set of labeled pairs. We'll help with evaluation harness.
[00:15:55] Lena: Quick recap of agreed actions...
[00:16:05] Lena: Marcus will provision the 10k rerank benchmark with 512/768/1536 dims, run hosted initial test then VPC test. I'll send pricing + security docs. Priya will share sample dataset.
[00:16:20] Priya: Sounds good.
[00:16:30] Tom: One more Q: SLOs for cold start on dedicated nodes?
[00:16:40] Marcus: Cold start for models in dedicated pools is minutes if model not warmed; for embeddings models it's usually seconds for warmup. We recommend keeping warm replicas for interactive lanes.
[00:16:55] Rajiv: Any advice on index refresh frequency? We have daily ingestion.
[00:17:05] Marcus: For daily ingestion you can rebuild overnight; for near-real-time delta updates use incremental indexing and memtables. Choice affects serving consistency and memory patterns.
[00:17:25] Anita: Okay that's helpful.
[00:17:35] Marcus: I'll note some pitfalls: 1) don't oversize batch for interactive lane; 2) measure recall delta when moving to 4-bit; 3) co-locate index & compute for latency SLOs.
[00:17:55] Lena: We'll follow up with a meeting invite for the benchmark review. Anything else?
[00:18:05] Priya: No, thank you.
[00:18:15] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[00:18:25] Lena: Thanks, bye.
[00:54:30] (call end)
